mentions.excerpt: Michael Burry, citing Apollo’s Torsten Slok, says private non-residential construction excluding data centers fell 7.9% year over year in June.
Torsten Slok, Apollo’s chief economist, turns the revenue question into an accounting test.
Torsten Slok’s earlier question was who would write the checks if technology companies’ cash flow doubled while their customers’ did not.

Torsten Slok’s fear that agents will move deposits from accounts earning the 0.1% national average to accounts yielding 3.3% to 5% is economically coherent, but Walker notes that cash-sorting fears have recurred at events including the SVB collapse and mostly failed to play out.
Torsten Slok of Apollo says adding technology analysts’ forecasts roughly doubles the sector’s operating cash flow to about $2.4 trillion by 2028, a gain of more than $1.2 trillion.
Torsten Slok and Burry tie the rate rise directly to the buildout.

sides.claim: Analysts covering tech expect the sector's operating cash flow to more than double to roughly $2.4 trillion by 2028, an increase of over $1.2 trillion, while analysts covering the other S&P 500 sectors, which are tech's customers, expect those…

The tech silo is betting on a future in which demand for AI and tech services explodes, while the silos covering the companies that would pay for those services see a much more modest outlook, and both cannot be right at the same time.

sides.question: whose-margin-pays
sides.claim: Agentic AI assistants like Muse could soon automatically sweep household cash into accounts paying 3.3% to 5.0%, instead of leaving it in checking accounts earning the 0.1% national average.

sides.question: who-writes-the-checks
sides.claim: Wall Street equity analysts work in sector silos, and adding up their forecasts produces internally inconsistent numbers.

sides.question: what-does-5-percent-do
sides.claim: Consensus expects hyperscalers' operating cash flow to more than triple by 2030, outpacing the sharp increase in AI-driven capex, based on FactSet and Apollo Chief Economist sources for Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Oracle.
